archive: The agency keeps its past here. Judging by the filing system, it would prefer not to discuss it.
An archive. Where a loose end becomes a reference number.
I should be precise. "Somewhere in a folder" is not a useful location in this room.
Paper leaves a trail. Provided nobody files the trail under "miscellaneous".
The silence is impressive. Even the accusations are in writing.
An old report can be more useful than a fresh confession. Fewer opportunities to improvise.
I came looking for answers. They will almost certainly require a document number.
Every file started with somebody saying this would be straightforward.
Nothing here is ancient history until I have checked the dates.
A missing document can mean something. So can a document that is suspiciously easy to find.
The truth is probably in here somewhere. I hope it knows its department.
Best leave everything where I found it. Accidentally tidying up could destroy the entire system.

archiveArchivist: Lieutenant Frank Drebin. I should approach with a clear question and correctly assembled paperwork.
Frank has the expression of a man who has already checked my attachments.
I suspect he can hear a missing page.
He does not look easily impressed. I shall start with legible handwriting.
A useful person to know. A dangerous person to hand an incomplete form.
Frank makes eye contact like he is checking a reference number.
I should keep my question brief. He appears to charge interest on unnecessary words.
An archivist remembers where things belong. Including visitors who should be elsewhere.

archivistAbsent: Frank is out. The files have declined to nominate a replacement.
No archivist. I should return later rather than develop an adventurous interpretation of access rights.
He is not here. Asking the room a question will only make this visit harder to explain.
Frank has left the archive unattended. That is not the same as leaving it open for inspection.
I need Frank, not merely the general concept of paperwork.
reportPending: First the report, then the questions. Frank has established an unusually clear agenda.
I need to print the mission report at the office computer and bring it here.
A successful investigation apparently remains a rumour until I deliver the paperwork.
He wants the printed report. Describing it enthusiastically will not count.
The office computer has MISSION REPORT. I should use that before attempting charm.
reportSubmitted: Report filed. My investigation now officially exists in a second location.
Frank accepted the attachments. I shall record that as restrained enthusiasm.
The report is in. Now I can ask a question without being mistaken for an administrative problem.
Filed successfully. A remarkably tense way to hand someone paper.
One report delivered. No pages missing, and only a small amount of dignity lost.
indexPuzzleOffered: Sort the index cards. Apparently this is what passes for building trust.
Match the documents to their departments. I should follow the instructions, not my feelings about the departments.
Frank has offered me work with no travel involved. There must be a catch.
A little filing assistance. I should remember how often "a little" appears in incident reports.
The index cards can wait. Frank specifically said so. I may need that in writing.
duplicateFound: JM-041 appears twice. I should ask Frank before deciding what that means.
A duplicate entry. Possibly routine. Possibly the reason routine is worth checking.
Two entries, one reference number. A question, not yet an answer.
I found a discrepancy. Best preserve the details before my imagination improves them.
JM-041. I should remember the number and let Frank explain the duplication.
duplicateDiscussed: John McClane's field report. One number, two storage locations. I need to follow the ordinary records first.
The restricted copy is a lead, not permission. Frank made that distinction unusually clear.
Someone separated access to the same report. That tells me where to look, not what happened.
Ordinary records first. A sensible instruction, despite the deeply unhelpful word "ordinary".
I know more about where the report went. What happened to McClane is still a separate question.
wrongItem: That was not the report. An important distinction I should have made before the presentation.
Frank requested documentation. I have attempted interpretation.
I should check what I am holding before calling it supporting evidence.
The wrong item. Confidence remains an unreliable filing method.
I need the actual mission report. Frank is not accepting substitutes, symbolic or otherwise.
